newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Death toll in Pakistan train crash rises to 136.
newsitem.headline: Death toll in Pakistan train crash rises to 136.

text.p: The death toll from Pakistan's worst train crash in seven years rose to 136 on Tuesday after some of the 90 injured died, doctors said.

A passenger express train, apparently with defective brakes, crashed near the town of Khanewal in the central province of Punjab on Monday after being switched to a dead-end line to avert a head-on collision with the Karachi-Lahore express.

Two of the five coaches derailed by the impact were completely crushed, trapping the dead and dying in a maze of twisted metal. Many passengers had been asleep when the accident occurred at about 4 a.m. (2300 GMT Sunday).

President Farooq Leghari, during a visit to injured passengers in a hospital in Multan, about 45 km (28 miles) west of Khanewal, said it was not clear if sabotage or brake failure was behind the crash.
"Nobody knows yet whether it is an act of sabotage or not," Leghari said.

"In any case, it is failure of the system, whether from sabotage or because of other faults, and this should not have been the case. It is the right of our people that they travel safely, whether by rail or by buses," he told reporters.
"All things would be thoroughly probed and after that we will be in a position to say if sabotage took place or not," Leghari said. He did not say who might have sabotaged the train or why.
Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif, who flew to Khanewal on Monday, has ordered an inquiry into the crash, saying railway authorities would not be spared if negligence was detected.

The inquiry would be conducted by Muhammad Afzal, the Federal Government Inspector of Railways, the official news agency APP reported. It said the driver and fireman of the runaway train had both survived the crash. APP said it was the fifth rail accident near Khanewal this year. Among the injured were a four-year-old girl who had lost her mother and a newlywed whose bride had died, it said.
The Deputy Commissioner of Khanewal, Haseeb Athar, told Reuters by telephone he would submit a preliminary report on the tragedy on Tuesday. "Salvage work is still going on," he added.
A Pakistan Air Force Hercules C-130 transport plane was due to fly the bodies of the victims from the city of Multan to their home towns later on Tuesday, officials said.

Monday's crash was the deadliest rail accident in Pakistan since January 3, 1990, when a passenger train ploughed into a stationary freight train at Sangi railway station in Sindh province, killing 307 people and injuring 400.
